items.title: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean
items.claim: What does standard deviation tell you?

options.text: The highest value in the data
The typical (root mean square) deviation from the mean — about 68% of normally distributed data lies within one SD of the mean, 95% within two SD, 99.7% within three SD

items.reveal:
Standard deviation σ is calculated as the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean. For a normal distribution, the 68-95-99.7 rule applies — though many geographical datasets are not normal (skewed by extremes).

In fieldwork: comparing pebble sizes on two beaches, two questionnaire response distributions, or rainfall variability at two stations. A small SD means data cluster near the mean; a large SD means high variability.

Coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean) allows comparison between datasets with different means — useful when comparing variability across scales.
items.why: Statistical literacy underpins geographical analysis. Reporting only a mean hides whether the data are tightly clustered or wildly variable — and the difference often matters more than the mean itself.

items.title: Longshore drift can move entire beaches kilometres

options.text: It moves sand offshore into deep water
Wave-driven net sediment transport along the coast in the direction of prevailing waves — building spits (Spurn, Dawlish Warren) and stripping beaches downdrift of groynes
It mixes salt and freshwater at estuaries
It transports sediment upstream in rivers

items.reveal:
Swash hits the beach at an angle (the angle of incoming waves) and backwash returns straight downslope under gravity. Net effect: sediment moves along the coast, often metres per day for fine sand.

Spurn Head (Yorkshire) is a 5 km spit built by longshore drift carrying sediment from Holderness cliffs (eroding at up to 2 m/year) southward. The cliffs supply around 1 million m³ of sediment per year.

Groynes trap drift on their up-drift side and starve beaches on the down-drift side — a coastal management trade-off.
items.why: Coastal protection in one place can damage another. Sediment budgets are zero-sum: a beach kept by groynes is sand denied to the next beach down the coast.

items.title: The Amazon generates much of its own rainfall
items.claim: How much of South American rainfall depends on Amazon transpiration?

options.text: None — rainfall comes entirely from the Atlantic

Amazon trees transpire huge volumes of water vapour, recycling moisture 5-6 times across the basin and generating 'flying rivers' that supply rainfall to southeast South America — including Brazil's agricultural heartland

items.reveal:
A mature Amazon tree can transpire 200-1,000 litres per day. The 'flying river' concept, popularised through INPE (Brazilian space agency) research and Antonio Nobre's work, describes the moisture flux from the basin southward — equivalent to or exceeding the Amazon River's surface discharge.

Deforestation reduces transpiration. Gatti et al. (Nature 2021) showed that the southern and eastern Amazon are already becoming net carbon sources. A tipping point at around 20-25% deforestation could shift large parts of the forest to savannah — with major consequences for Brazilian rainfall and agriculture.

Current deforestation is around 17-20% of the original Amazon area.
items.why: Forests are climate machines. Amazon loss would change rainfall patterns far beyond the basin — and threaten the agricultural economy that has driven much of the deforestation in the first place.
